headline: North Rip Green and Ripping — Bonito Committed, Bass Still Playing Coy
subhead: The bait is thick, the water's clean, and the fleet is watching the moon build toward full for the first real fall trigger.
body_markdown:
There's a change in the air out here that you feel before you can point to it on a chart. The nights have started to carry a little bite to them, the wind's swinging more out of the north on the mornings, and out on the water the bait has that nervous, balled-up look it gets right before things start happening for real. Block Island in early September doesn't announce itself — it leans into you a little at a time, and this week it leaned hard.

The bonito showed up in real numbers, and they showed up right on schedule. Southwest Ledge has had them working the rips on the last of the ebb, chasing bay anchovies and rain bait so small that standard metal has been getting refused half the time. The fleet's been downsizing — quarter-ounce epoxy jigs in olive-over-white, small Deceivers, anything with a slim profile — and that's what's been connecting. North Rip has had the same story on the change of tide, green water, current stacking bait against the structure, bonito slashing through it in those quick, hard-to-predict pushes that make you burn a lot of gas for a few good minutes of work. That westward push everyone's been tracking is real — Point Judith's getting them now too, and the word out of Fishers Island Sound and the Race is that the pattern's spreading fast. We flagged the false albacore to follow the bonito within a week or two of that push starting, and while nobody's called albies in numbers yet, the timing lines up — worth checking the rips daily from here out, because that's usually how it goes once the bonito get established.

Striped bass are the harder read right now. There's plenty of bait around — bunker are thickening up in Narragansett Bay the same way they are on the mainland side — but the water's still sitting in that low-to-mid 70s range that keeps bass more interested in staying loose on the bait than committing to a real blitz. Southwest Ledge has still been giving up fish on the drop of the tide, working live eels and bunker chunks down deep, 25 to 40 feet, right where the ledge breaks off into the deeper water. Nothing has come easy this week — it's been a fish here, a fish there, mostly at first light or the last hour of daylight when the light drops and the bigger fish push up onto the structure. We said last week that the trigger for the first real blitz activity would be bait density tightening up as the moon builds and the tide flow increases, and that's exactly the pattern setting up now. The moon's building toward full on the 6th and 7th, which should start squeezing those bunker schools tighter over the next several days. Combine that with the first real cool front, and there's a good chance the switch flips on Narragansett Bay and around the island within the next week to ten days. Until then, treat the Ledge and the North Rip as places where a handful of quality fish are still very catchable, not a guaranteed blitz.

Bluefish have been the most dependable thing going. We called this one too — said the warm water would keep them aggressive through Labor Day week, and that's held up. Choppers in the 4 to 8 pound class have been running hard on bunker schools off Newport and in the rips around the island, and topwater poppers and diamond jigs with wire leader have been getting bit steadily through the middle of the day, not just the classic dawn-and-dusk windows. If you want fast action without overthinking the tide, this has been the most consistent bite on the whole beat.

Fluke are winding down the way they always do this time of year. The back bay fish have mostly cleared out for deeper structure, and while there are still keeper-class fish being picked off around deeper rock piles and current-swept bottom off the island, the bite has thinned out noticeably compared to a month ago. If fluke is the goal, this is the week to fish the deeper edges early in the day before the bite shuts down with the sun.

Looking ahead, the next few days should hold close to what we've already seen — bonito active on the tide changes at Southwest Ledge and North Rip, bluefish reliable on the bunker schools, and bass fishable but not yet blitzing. If the wind stays out of the north and the nights keep cooling the way they have been, expect that first real fall trigger for the stripers to start showing itself right around the full moon, with Narragansett Bay and the mouth of the Bay the most likely places for it to break open first. Until then, the smart play is working the tide changes on the rips for bonito and bluefish, and treating the bass bite as a low-light, structure-specific game rather than an all-day proposition. That should change soon — but it hasn't changed yet, and there's no sense pretending otherwise.
